title: Preverb-Verb Inversion Under Focus and Negation

sections.title: Why the Preverb Moves Behind the Verb
sections.content: In neutral affirmative clauses, the verbal prefix (igekötő)—such as meg-, el-, ki-, be-, fel-, rá-—occupies the pre-verbal slot attached directly to the verb: 'Megértettem a helyzetet' (I understood the situation). When a focused phrase or the negation particle 'nem/sem' claims that pre-verbal slot, the preverb is pushed immediately behind the conjugated verb: 'Én értettem meg a helyzetet' (It was I who understood the situation).

sections.title: Contrastive Pairs in Literary Prose
sections.content: Writers constantly alternate between unsplit verbs (moving the plot forward) and inverted verbs (analyzing motives, causes, and exceptions).

sections.title: Neutral vs. Focused Preverb Order
rows: It was Ákos who broke the silence.
He/she did not break the silence.
Rádöbbent az igazságra. -> Későn döbbent rá az igazságra.
He realized the truth. -> It was late that he realized the truth.

items.spanish: Egyikük sem merte megtörni a hallgatást, végül Ákos szólalt meg.
items.english: Neither of them dared break the silence; finally it was Ákos who spoke up.

items.spanish: Nem a fáradtságtól sápadt el, hanem a hirtelen bűntudattól.
items.english: It was not from fatigue that he turned pale, but from sudden guilt.

items.spanish: A vendéglőben ébredtek rá, mennyire hiányzott nekik a társaság.
items.english: It was in the restaurant that they realized how much they had missed company.

sections.title: B2 Stylistic Notice
sections.content: Whenever you see 'Verb + Preverb' (e.g., 'szólalt meg', 'vette észre', 'döbbent rá'), look at the word immediately to the left of the verb—that word carries the sentence's primary stress and focal meaning.
